Phebe (Phoebe)
FEE-bee
proper noun (person)
Greek Phoibe, "bright, radiant"; a servant of the church at Cenchrea, commended by Paul, likely the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Phebe was a Christian woman of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth, whom the apostle Paul commended in the closing chapter of his Epistle to the Romans, and who is widely believed to have carried that letter to Rome. "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: that ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:1-2). The word translated "servant" (Greek diakonos) marks her as one who ministered in the practical service of the church, and "succourer" (a patroness or helper) shows she had given generous aid to many believers and to Paul himself. Paul honored her by name, asked the Roman church to receive and assist her, and entrusted to her, it seems, the most weighty doctrinal letter of the New Testament. Phebe stands in the dictionary as a faithful servant and helper of the church, a witness to the honored and vital ministry of godly women in the service, hospitality, and support of the saints, exercised within the good order God has appointed, and a model of the practical love that succours many for Christ's sake.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A servant (diakonos) and "succourer" of the church at Cenchrea (Rom 16:1-2), commended by Paul and likely the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans; a model of the honored ministry of godly women in serving and aiding the saints.

Commended by Paul to the church at Rome.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:1 — "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:"

Rom 16:2 — "That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also."

1 Tim 5:10 — "Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted..."

Titus 2:3 — "The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness... teachers of good things;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Phebe honors the recovery of the honored, vital ministry of godly women within biblical order, against both a feminism that demands the offices Scripture reserves and a neglect that overlooks the indispensable service of women in the church.

expand to see more

Women's-ministry-neglected correction. Some so guard the church's order that they overlook the rich and honored ministries Scripture gives to women. Paul commended Phebe by name, called her a servant and succourer of many, and entrusted her with his greatest letter. The dictionary holds that godly women have vital, honored ministries — hospitality, mercy, service, the support of gospel work, the teaching of younger women (Titus 2:3-5) — and that the church which fails to recognize and value such service is poorer for it.

This entry faces a real postmodern pressure. Some press Phebe's title diakonos to overturn the biblical reservation of the teaching and ruling offices of the church to qualified men. The dictionary holds the complementarian order of Scripture: women serve in countless honored ways, as Phebe did, but the offices of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are entrusted to men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). To honor Phebe rightly is to honor both her real and commended ministry and the good order within which she served, refusing to set her example against the Word that records it.
